note:
Visit modality: audio-only telephone visit, about 25 minutes. The patient is a 75-year-old male with a changing pigmented lesion on his upper back. History was obtained from the patient and from his daughter, who is his caregiver and stayed on the line for the whole call. Video was not possible because he has no smartphone and the home internet connection is unreliable.

Reason for visit: The daughter noticed a dark spot on his right upper back that has gotten bigger and darker. The patient cannot see his own back and had not noticed it. She first estimated that it had been changing for about 3 months, then corrected herself after checking the date stamp on an older photo on her phone and said it has really been closer to 6 months. She describes it as dark brown to black with an uneven edge and a lighter pink area along one side. The patient denies pain, itching, or bleeding from the spot. He denies any drainage or open sore. He denies fever, weight loss, and night sweats, and has not noticed new lumps in his neck or armpits. The daughter has not seen other new or changing spots when she helps him bathe, but she has not looked closely at his scalp or feet.

Skin history: A basal cell carcinoma of the left temple was removed with Mohs surgery about 4 years ago. He farmed outdoors for decades and had many sunburns as a young man. No personal history of melanoma. His brother had melanoma in his sixties.

Other conditions: atrial fibrillation, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and chronic kidney disease stage 3a. No known drug allergies.

Medications, reviewed with the daughter reading from the bottles: Apixaban, which she first said was 2.5 mg twice daily; after reading the label she corrected this to 5 mg twice daily. Metformin 500 mg twice daily. Lisinopril 20 mg daily, increased from 10 mg by his PCP about 6 weeks ago. Atorvastatin 40 mg at bedtime. Metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily. Aspirin 81 mg was stopped by cardiology when the apixaban was started, and the daughter confirmed he no longer takes it.

Data reviewed: Recent labs from his PCP show creatinine 1.3, eGFR 54, A1c 7.1%, and hemoglobin 13.2. Home readings this morning per the daughter were BP 138/78, pulse 72, and fingerstick glucose 128. The daughter uploaded two photos to the patient portal before the call, which I reviewed during the visit. They show a single lesion of about 9 mm with dark brown to black color, an irregular border, and a pink area along one edge. The photos are taken in room light without dermoscopy, so they cannot replace an in-person exam, and no total body skin exam was possible by phone.

Transportation: He does not drive. The daughter works full time and lives an hour away, and the clinic is about 40 miles from his home. He missed two earlier dermatology visits because no ride was available, and the daughter says that each trip means taking a full day off work.

Impression: Changing pigmented lesion of the right upper back with enlargement, color variation, and border irregularity, suspicious for melanoma until proven otherwise. The differential includes a dysplastic nevus and a pigmented basal cell carcinoma. This needs a biopsy and should not wait for a routine appointment.

Next steps, discussed with the patient and his daughter, who both agreed:
- In-person visit within 2 weeks for a full skin exam and same-day excisional biopsy, so that he needs only one trip. We will try to book it on the same day as his cardiology follow-up in the same building.
- Referral to clinic social work to arrange a medical transportation benefit or a volunteer driver. I will call the daughter back with the ride options.
- Continue apixaban 5 mg twice daily; a small skin biopsy does not require holding it. Continue the other medications unchanged.
- Daughter to upload new photos with a ruler beside the lesion and to check his scalp and feet.
- Sun protection advice reviewed. Call sooner if the spot bleeds, forms a sore, or grows quickly.
- If pathology confirms melanoma, referral to dermatologic surgery for wide excision.
- Phone check in 1 week to confirm the ride and the appointment.
summary: A 75-year-old male was seen by telephone, with his daughter assisting as caregiver, for a changing pigmented lesion on his right upper back that has become bigger and darker over about 6 months. He denies pain, itching, bleeding, fever, and weight loss, and has a history of basal cell carcinoma, atrial fibrillation, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and chronic kidney disease. Photos reviewed by the clinician show a lesion of about 9 mm with an irregular border and color variation, and the impression is suspicion for melanoma. Because transportation is a barrier, an in-person visit with same-day biopsy will be arranged with social work help for rides, apixaban will continue, and a phone check is planned in 1 week.

note:
Doctor: Thanks for coming in. I have your records here. You are a 28-year-old female, and you were in the hospital about three weeks ago for appendicitis, correct?

Patient: Yes, I had my appendix out. They told me the scan showed something on my adrenal gland, and I got scared.

Doctor: That is common, and it is usually harmless. The CT showed a 1.8 centimeter nodule on the right adrenal gland, and the radiologist described it as low density, which is reassuring. Still, we need to check whether it makes extra hormones. Have you had headaches, a racing heart, or sweating spells?

Patient: No headaches, no racing heart, no sweating spells.

Doctor: Any weight gain, easy bruising, or purple stretch marks?

Patient: No, none of that.

Doctor: Any high blood pressure that you know of?

Patient: No, it has always been normal.

Doctor: Good. Your blood pressure today is 116/72 and your heart rate is 70. Your face looks normal, and I don't see any purple stretch marks. Are you taking any medicines?

Patient: Just a birth control pill every day.

Doctor: That can affect one of the tests, so I will take it into account. Here is what we will do. Tonight at 11 you take a 1 mg dexamethasone pill, and tomorrow morning we draw a cortisol level. We will also check plasma metanephrines and an aldosterone and renin level. The nodule looks benign, so I don't need more scans right now. My impression is an adrenal incidentaloma without any signs of hormone excess so far. Come back in three weeks and we will go over the results.

Patient: Okay, that sounds good.
summary: A 28-year-old female was seen in endocrinology clinic about three weeks after a hospital stay for appendicitis, during which a CT found a 1.8 centimeter right adrenal nodule. She denies headaches, racing heart, sweating spells, weight gain, easy bruising, and stretch marks, and her blood pressure is 116/72. The impression is an adrenal incidentaloma without signs of hormone excess so far. A dexamethasone suppression test, plasma metanephrines, and aldosterone and renin levels were ordered, with a return visit in three weeks.

soap.subjective: Referred after a hospitalization about three weeks ago for appendicitis, treated with appendix removal, during which a scan showed an adrenal finding. Denies headaches, racing heart, sweating spells, weight gain, easy bruising, and purple stretch marks. No known high blood pressure. Takes a birth control pill every day.
soap.objective: Blood pressure 116/72, heart rate 70. Face looks normal and no purple stretch marks seen. CT showed a 1.8 centimeter nodule on the right adrenal gland described by the radiologist as low density.
soap.assessment: Adrenal incidentaloma, a 1.8 centimeter right adrenal nodule that looks benign, without signs of hormone excess so far.
plan: 1 mg dexamethasone taken tonight at 11, with a morning cortisol level drawn tomorrow
Check plasma metanephrines and an aldosterone and renin level
No additional imaging right now because the nodule looks benign
Birth control pill noted as a possible effect on one of the tests and will be taken into account
Return in three weeks to review results

note:
Hospital day 3 for a 79-year-old female with Parkinson disease who was admitted with a urinary tract infection and worsening gait freezing. No overnight events. She has had no falls on the ward and denies hallucinations, confusion, and trouble swallowing. She reports that her right hand tremor and stiffness return in the mid-afternoon, about an hour before her next dose, and that her walking is slower during those periods.

Medication reconciliation with the pharmacist clarified what she takes at home. Her prescribed medicines are carbidopa-levodopa 25/100 mg one tablet three times daily and pramipexole 0.25 mg three times daily. She also buys over-the-counter supplements without telling her doctors: ferrous sulfate 325 mg once daily, which she takes together with her morning carbidopa-levodopa dose, and ginkgo biloba, which she takes for memory. Iron can reduce levodopa absorption, which may be contributing to her morning and afternoon off periods. She denies orthostatic lightheadedness.

Current inpatient medications are ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily, carbidopa-levodopa, and pramipexole as above.

Exam this morning: vitals BP 128/74, HR 76, temperature 98.2 F, RR 16, SpO2 96% on room air. She is alert and oriented. Mild resting tremor of the right hand, cogwheel rigidity in the right arm, bradykinesia, and a slow shuffling gait with difficulty turning. No dyskinesias. No suprapubic tenderness.

Data: Urine culture grew E. coli sensitive to ceftriaxone. WBC 8.4, down from 12.1 on admission. Creatinine 0.9. Hemoglobin 11.8.

Impression: Parkinson disease with end-of-dose wearing off, likely worsened by iron taken with levodopa and by the acute infection. E. coli urinary tract infection, improving. Mild anemia, which is probably why she started the iron on her own.

Changes and recommendations today: Increase carbidopa-levodopa 25/100 mg to one tablet four times daily, with the doses spaced evenly through the day. Stop ferrous sulfate and ginkgo biloba for now; if iron is still needed after an outpatient anemia work-up, it should be taken at least 2 hours away from levodopa. Continue pramipexole 0.25 mg three times daily. Continue ceftriaxone today, then change to cephalexin 500 mg twice daily to complete 7 days of treatment. Physical therapy and occupational therapy to evaluate gait and fall risk. Anticipate discharge tomorrow with neurology follow-up in 4 weeks.
summary: A 79-year-old female with Parkinson disease is on hospital day 3 for a urinary tract infection and worsening gait freezing, with right hand tremor and stiffness returning before her next dose. Pharmacy review found she takes over-the-counter ferrous sulfate with her morning carbidopa-levodopa and also uses ginkgo biloba. Exam showed a resting tremor, cogwheel rigidity, bradykinesia, and a shuffling gait, and urine culture grew E. coli with improving white count. Carbidopa-levodopa was increased to four times daily, the supplements were stopped, ceftriaxone will be changed to cephalexin, and therapy evaluations and neurology follow-up were arranged.

57-year-old female, urgent care, ID eval for painful rash. Recent admission within past month.

CC: painful blistering rash R flank/back x 4 d
- Burning/stabbing pain R mid-back wrapping toward R upper abd started ~6 d ago, rash appeared 4 d ago (pt first said 3 d, then corrected to 4 d)
- Pain 7/10, worse w/ clothing touching skin, poor sleep
- Rash = clusters of vesicles on red base, stays on R side, does not cross midline
- Denies fever, chills, headache, vision change, eye pain, ear pain, facial droop
- Denies leg weakness, urinary retention, new confusion
- Denies new SOB beyond baseline COPD
- No known contact w/ chickenpox. Never had Shingrix. Chickenpox as a child per pt

Recent hosp: admitted ~3 wk ago w/ COPD exac, 5 d stay, d/c'd on prednisone 40 mg x 5 d burst (finished ~10 d ago). No ICU, no intubation.

PMH: COPD, T2DM, HTN, CKD stage 3b, hyperlipidemia
NKDA

- metformin 1000 mg BID
- lisinopril 20 mg daily
- atorvastatin 40 mg qhs
- tiotropium 18 mcg inhaled daily
- albuterol 2 puffs q4-6h PRN
- ibuprofen 800 mg TID for the pain per pt, correction: bottle says 400 mg TID

- Gen: uncomfortable, NAD at rest
- Skin: grouped vesicles w/ some crusting on erythematous base, R T8 dermatome, mid-back to R upper abd, does not cross midline; no purulence, no surrounding warmth

- Lungs: scattered mild exp wheeze, no resp distress (baseline)

1. Herpes zoster R T8 dermatome, no ophthalmic/otic/motor involvement, no secondary infection
2. Zoster pain; ibuprofen not appropriate w/ CKD stage 3b + lisinopril
3. T2DM; eGFR 44 so metformin needs dose reduction; glucose up after recent steroid burst

- START gabapentin 100 mg TID, PCP can titrate

The diagnosis is herpes zoster, treated with valacyclovir, gabapentin, and acetaminophen, with ibuprofen stopped, metformin reduced to 500 mg BID for her kidney function, and PCP follow-up in 1 week with return precautions.

note:
Doctor: Good evening. I understand you've had belly pain for a couple of days. I see here you are a 79-year-old male. Tell me what has been going on.

Patient: It started two days ago around my belly button, kind of a dull ache. Yesterday it moved down to the right side, low, and now it hurts a lot when I walk or cough.

Doctor: Any nausea or vomiting?

Patient: I feel sick to my stomach and I threw up once this morning. I haven't wanted to eat anything.

Doctor: Any fever or chills? Diarrhea, blood in your stool, or trouble passing urine?

Patient: I felt warm last night but I didn't check. No diarrhea, no blood in the stool. My urine is fine, even with the prostate problem.

Doctor: Any chest pain or shortness of breath?

Patient: No, nothing like that.

Doctor: What medicines do you take?

Patient: Lisinopril 10 mg every morning for my high blood pressure, tamsulosin 0.4 mg at night for the prostate, and a baby aspirin 81 mg daily.

Doctor: Okay. Your vitals here are blood pressure 148/84, heart rate 92, and temperature 100.1 F. On exam you are tender in the right lower quadrant, with guarding there, and it hurts on the right when I press on the left side. Your blood work shows a white count of 14.8, and your kidney function is normal with a creatinine of 1.1. The CT scan with contrast shows your appendix is swollen at 12 millimeters with inflammation around it, but no rupture and no abscess.

Patient: So is it my appendix?

Doctor: Yes, this is acute appendicitis. I am calling the surgeon to see you. We are giving you ceftriaxone 2 g and metronidazole 500 mg through the IV right now, and I will order something for the pain. Please don't eat or drink anything for now. I am also holding your lisinopril tonight, since you may be going to the operating room.

Patient: Will I need surgery?

Doctor: Most likely a laparoscopic appendectomy, and the surgeon will talk with you about it. We will admit you to the hospital.

Patient: All right.
summary: A 79-year-old male came to the emergency department with two days of abdominal pain that began around the umbilicus and moved to the right lower quadrant, with nausea and one episode of vomiting. He denies diarrhea, blood in the stool, urinary trouble, chest pain, and shortness of breath. He is tender in the right lower quadrant with a white count of 14.8, and CT showed an inflamed appendix without rupture. The diagnosis is acute appendicitis, and he received IV ceftriaxone and metronidazole, lisinopril was held, and surgery was consulted for likely laparoscopic appendectomy and admission.

soap.subjective: Two days of dull periumbilical abdominal pain that moved to the low right side and is worse with walking and coughing. Nausea, one episode of vomiting this morning, and poor appetite. Felt warm last night without checking a temperature. Denies diarrhea, blood in the stool, trouble passing urine, chest pain, and shortness of breath. History of high blood pressure and a prostate problem. Home medications: lisinopril 10 mg every morning, tamsulosin 0.4 mg at night, baby aspirin 81 mg daily.
soap.objective: Blood pressure 148/84, heart rate 92, temperature 100.1 F. Tender in the right lower quadrant with guarding, and right-sided pain when the left side is pressed. White count 14.8, creatinine 1.1. CT scan with contrast shows a swollen 12 millimeter appendix with surrounding inflammation, no rupture, and no abscess.
soap.assessment: Acute appendicitis without rupture or abscess on CT.
plan: Ceftriaxone 2 g and metronidazole 500 mg IV now
Pain medication ordered
Nothing to eat or drink
Hold lisinopril tonight in case of surgery
Surgical consultation for likely laparoscopic appendectomy
Admit to the hospital

note:
Doctor: Good morning, and thanks for coming in. I have your chart here. You are an 81-year-old male, and your primary doctor sent you to talk about colon cancer screening. Is that right?

Patient: Yes, he said I'm overdue. I think my last colonoscopy was about five years ago.

Doctor: Let me look at the report. It says here your last colonoscopy was about ten years ago, and it was normal.

Patient: Ten? You know, you're right. My wife had hers five years ago and I mixed us up. Mine was ten years ago.

Doctor: No problem. Have you noticed any blood in your stool, black stools, a change in your bowel habits, or belly pain?

Patient: No blood, no black stools, my bowels are regular, and no belly pain.

Doctor: Any weight loss that you did not intend?

Patient: No, my weight has been steady.

Doctor: Any family history of colon cancer?

Patient: My father had it, in his seventies.

Doctor: Okay. Tell me about your health overall and your medicines.

Patient: I have A-fib, congestive heart failure, high blood pressure, and diabetes. I take Eliquis 5 mg twice a day, furosemide 40 mg every morning, which my cardiologist raised from 20 mg last month, metoprolol succinate 50 mg every day, metformin 500 mg twice a day, and a baby aspirin 81 mg every day. I also take ibuprofen 600 mg three times a day for my knees.

Doctor: Thank you. And how much alcohol do you drink in a day?

Patient: Oh, a couple of beers. Maybe two.

Doctor: I ask everyone this carefully, because it changes my advice. Is two a typical day?

Patient: Well... honestly it's closer to six beers a day. I didn't want to say. Not two, six.

Doctor: Thank you for being honest with me. Now your exam and results. Your blood pressure is 134/78 and your pulse is 70 and irregular. Your belly is soft and not tender, I can't feel an enlarged liver, and I don't see any yellowing of the eyes or swelling in your legs. Your labs from last week show a hemoglobin of 13.4, so you are not anemic. Your platelets are a little low at 142, your creatinine is 1.2, and your liver enzyme AST is a bit high at 58.

Patient: Is that bad?

Doctor: It tells me the alcohol is affecting your liver, and we will follow up on that. Now, about screening. You are 81, with heart failure and A-fib, you take a blood thinner, and you drink heavily. A colonoscopy needs a bowel prep that can dry you out while you are on a water pill, sedation carries more risk with your heart, and removing a polyp could cause bleeding on Eliquis. Your last colonoscopy was normal ten years ago, and the guidelines say that after 75 screening is an individual decision and after 85 we generally stop. A slow-growing polyp may never bother you in your lifetime. A safer choice is a stool test called a FIT. If it is positive, we would talk about a colonoscopy together with your cardiologist.

Patient: I'd rather do the stool test. I don't want that prep again.

Doctor: Good, I will give you a FIT kit to do at home. Second, ibuprofen and aspirin together with Eliquis raise your risk of a stomach bleed, and the alcohol adds to it. I want you to stop the ibuprofen and the baby aspirin. For your knees you can take Tylenol 500 mg two or three times a day, but no more than 2 grams a day because of your liver.

Patient: The aspirin was for my heart, though.

Doctor: Since you take Eliquis, the aspirin usually isn't needed, and I will send a note to your cardiologist to confirm. Third is the alcohol. Six beers a day can scar the liver and raises your risk of bleeding and falls. I am ordering a liver ultrasound, a FibroScan to check for scarring, and a repeat hepatic panel. I am starting thiamine 100 mg every day, and I am referring you to our addiction medicine clinic. Please don't stop drinking suddenly on your own, because withdrawal can be dangerous. Call us first and we will help you cut down safely.

Patient: I'll try. My wife keeps asking me to.

Doctor: Good. My impression is that you do not need a screening colonoscopy for now, you will do the FIT at home, and you have heavy alcohol use with probable alcohol-related liver injury. Let's meet again in three months, or sooner if you see blood in your stool.

Patient: Thank you, doctor.
summary: An 81-year-old male was seen in gastroenterology clinic to discuss colon cancer screening; his last colonoscopy about ten years ago was normal. He denies blood in the stool, black stools, belly pain, and weight loss, has A-fib, heart failure, hypertension, and diabetes, and corrected his alcohol intake from two to about six beers a day. Labs showed hemoglobin 13.4, platelets 142, and AST 58. Given his age, comorbidities, anticoagulation, and drinking, the physician advised a home FIT test rather than colonoscopy, stopped ibuprofen and aspirin, started thiamine, and ordered a liver ultrasound, FibroScan, hepatic panel, and addiction medicine referral, with follow-up in three months.

soap.subjective: Referred by his primary doctor for colon cancer screening. Last colonoscopy was about ten years ago and normal (he first said five years ago, then corrected this). Denies blood in the stool, black stools, change in bowel habits, belly pain, and unintended weight loss. Father had colon cancer in his seventies. History of A-fib, congestive heart failure, high blood pressure, and diabetes. Medications: Eliquis 5 mg twice a day, furosemide 40 mg every morning (raised from 20 mg by his cardiologist last month), metoprolol succinate 50 mg every day, metformin 500 mg twice a day, baby aspirin 81 mg every day, and ibuprofen 600 mg three times a day for his knees. Alcohol: first reported two beers a day, then corrected to about six beers a day.
soap.objective: Blood pressure 134/78, pulse 70 and irregular. Abdomen soft and not tender, no enlarged liver felt, no yellowing of the eyes, no leg swelling. Labs from last week: hemoglobin 13.4, platelets 142 (a little low), creatinine 1.2, AST 58 (a bit high).
soap.assessment: Colon cancer screening discussion in an 81-year-old with a normal colonoscopy about ten years ago, heart failure, A-fib on a blood thinner, and heavy alcohol use; routine screening colonoscopy not advised for now. Heavy alcohol use with probable alcohol-related liver injury.
plan: No screening colonoscopy for now; FIT kit to be done at home, with colonoscopy discussed together with his cardiologist if positive
Stop ibuprofen and baby aspirin because of bleeding risk with Eliquis and alcohol; note to his cardiologist to confirm aspirin is not needed
Tylenol 500 mg two or three times a day for knee pain, no more than 2 grams a day
Liver ultrasound, FibroScan, and repeat hepatic panel
Start thiamine 100 mg every day
Referral to addiction medicine clinic; do not stop drinking suddenly without calling first
Follow up in three months, or sooner if blood appears in the stool

note:
Doctor: Hello, I'm the emergency physician. I understand your lips and face swelled up today. I see you are a 70-year-old female. What happened?

Patient: I was having dinner at a restaurant, shrimp pasta, and about twenty minutes later my lips started tingling and then swelling. Then I got hives on my chest and arms. My neighbor drove me straight here.

Doctor: Have you eaten shrimp before?

Patient: Yes, many times, and never had a problem.

Doctor: Any trouble breathing, wheezing, or throat tightness?

Patient: My throat felt a little tight at first, but I can breathe fine now. No wheezing.

Doctor: Any vomiting, belly cramps, dizziness, or fainting?

Patient: I felt a bit nauseated but I didn't vomit. No dizziness, no fainting, and no chest pain.

Doctor: Do you take any new medicines or supplements? Are you on a blood pressure pill like an ACE inhibitor?

Patient: No new medicines. I take amlodipine 5 mg every morning for my blood pressure and levothyroxine 75 mcg for my thyroid. That's all.

Doctor: Okay. Your blood pressure is 152/88, heart rate 98, respiratory rate 20, and temperature 98.4 F. I see swelling of your upper and lower lip and mild swelling of your tongue, hives on your chest and arms, but your voice is normal, there is no stridor, and your lungs are clear. This is an allergic reaction to the shrimp with angioedema. I gave you epinephrine 0.3 mg in the thigh muscle, and through the IV famotidine 20 mg and methylprednisolone 125 mg, plus cetirizine 10 mg by mouth. We drew a tryptase level as well.

Patient: Is it going to get worse?

Doctor: The swelling is already going down after the epinephrine. I want to watch you for six hours because the reaction can come back. If you stay stable, you can go home tonight.

Patient: How will I get home? My neighbor had to leave, and I live 45 minutes away. I don't drive at night and there is no bus after nine.

Doctor: Thank you for telling me. I will ask our social worker to arrange a taxi voucher for the ride home. I also want to fill your prescriptions in our outpatient pharmacy before you leave, because it is hard for you to make a second trip. You will get an epinephrine auto-injector 0.3 mg to carry with you, prednisone 40 mg once a day for three days, and cetirizine 10 mg every day for a week. Use the auto-injector if your lips or throat swell again and then call 911.

Patient: Okay.

Doctor: Avoid all shrimp and shellfish until you see an allergist. Because getting to a clinic is hard, we will set up a video visit with allergy, and a nurse will call you in two days to check on you. Come back right away for trouble breathing, throat tightness, or swelling that returns.

Patient: Thank you.
summary: A 70-year-old female came to the emergency department with lip and facial swelling and hives about twenty minutes after eating shrimp pasta. She had brief throat tightness but denies wheezing, vomiting, dizziness, fainting, and chest pain, and exam showed lip and tongue swelling without stridor. The diagnosis is an allergic reaction to shrimp with angioedema, treated with epinephrine, famotidine, methylprednisolone, and cetirizine, with a tryptase level drawn. She will be observed for six hours, then discharged with an epinephrine auto-injector, prednisone, and cetirizine, a taxi voucher, a video allergy visit, and a nurse call because transportation is difficult.

soap.subjective: Lip tingling then swelling and hives on the chest and arms about twenty minutes after eating shrimp pasta at a restaurant. Throat felt a little tight at first but she can breathe fine now. Mild nausea. Has eaten shrimp many times without problems. Denies wheezing, vomiting, dizziness, fainting, and chest pain. No new medicines. Takes amlodipine 5 mg every morning and levothyroxine 75 mcg. Lives 45 minutes away, does not drive at night, and there is no bus after nine, so getting back to a clinic is hard.

soap.assessment: Allergic reaction to shrimp with angioedema, improving after treatment.
plan: Epinephrine 0.3 mg in the thigh muscle, famotidine 20 mg and methylprednisolone 125 mg IV, and cetirizine 10 mg by mouth given in the emergency department
Observe for six hours and discharge home if stable

Fill prescriptions in the outpatient pharmacy before she leaves
Discharge with epinephrine auto-injector 0.3 mg, prednisone 40 mg once a day for three days, and cetirizine 10 mg every day for a week

Return right away for trouble breathing, throat tightness, or returning swelling

note:
The patient is a 20-year-old male seen in the urology clinic for follow-up of a right kidney stone. Two weeks ago he was seen in the emergency department with right flank pain radiating to the groin, and a CT scan showed a 5 mm stone in the right distal ureter and a 4 mm non-obstructing stone in the left lower pole of the kidney. He was sent home on tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily and ibuprofen 400 mg every 6 hours as needed, with a urine strainer. He passed the stone 9 days ago after a day of severe pain and caught it in the strainer. Since then the right flank pain has resolved. He denies fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, visible blood in the urine, and burning with urination. He stopped the ibuprofen on his own after the stone passed and is still taking tamsulosin.

This is his first stone episode. He drinks about 3 cups of fluid a day, mostly coffee and soda, and eats a lot of salty processed food. About 4 months ago he started a vitamin C supplement 1000 mg daily and a daily protein shake for weight training. His father had kidney stones. He has no other medical conditions and takes no other medicines.

On exam today BP 122/74, HR 66, and temperature 98.2 F. He is well appearing. There is no costovertebral angle tenderness on either side, and the abdomen is soft and nontender.

Stone analysis of the passed stone returned calcium oxalate monohydrate. Urinalysis today shows 3 to 5 red blood cells per high power field, with no white cells and no nitrite. Creatinine is 0.9, and serum calcium and uric acid are within normal limits.

Impression: First episode of calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis with spontaneous passage of the right ureteral stone, plus a residual 4 mm non-obstructing left lower pole stone. Contributing factors are low fluid intake, high sodium intake from processed food, and a vitamin C supplement.

Recommendations: Stop tamsulosin now that the stone has passed, and stop the vitamin C supplement. Increase fluids to about 3 liters a day, cut back on salty processed food, keep normal dietary calcium, and moderate the protein shakes. Order a 24-hour urine collection for stone risk and a PTH level. Renal ultrasound in 6 months to follow the left stone. Ibuprofen only if needed for pain. Return sooner for fever, severe flank pain, or vomiting. Follow up in clinic in 3 months with the 24-hour urine results.

Tamsulosin and vitamin C were stopped, fluid and diet advice was given, and a 24-hour urine collection, PTH level, and renal ultrasound in 6 months were planned.

note:
Reason for consult: Chronic kidney disease stage 3b with a rise in creatinine. Requesting service: hospital medicine.

HPI: The patient is a 33-year-old male with chronic kidney disease stage 3b from IgA nephropathy, baseline creatinine 2.1. He returned 10 days ago from a 3-week trip abroad and was admitted yesterday with 3 days of watery diarrhea and poor oral intake. He denies blood in the stool, fever, decreased urine output, flank pain, and leg swelling. He took no NSAIDs. Home medications are losartan 50 mg daily and sodium bicarbonate 650 mg twice daily. No known drug allergies.

Exam: BP 118/72, HR 96, temperature 98.6 F. Dry mucous membranes, no edema, lungs clear.

Data: Creatinine 2.4 today, up from baseline 2.1. Potassium 4.8. Urinalysis shows trace protein and no blood. Stool studies are pending.

Impression: Chronic kidney disease stage 3b with mild prerenal worsening from volume loss due to diarrhea.

Recommendations: Hold losartan while he has diarrhea and poor oral intake, and restart it when he is eating and drinking normally. Give gentle IV fluids. Continue sodium bicarbonate 650 mg twice daily. Avoid NSAIDs and IV contrast. Recheck a basic metabolic panel in the morning. Outpatient nephrology follow-up in 2 weeks after discharge.

Losartan is held, gentle IV fluids are given, NSAIDs and IV contrast are to be avoided, and nephrology follow-up is planned after discharge.

note:
The patient is a 27-year-old female who presents with 2 days of burning with urination, urinary frequency, and urgency. She also describes mild pressure above the pubic bone. She denies fever, chills, flank pain, nausea, vomiting, vaginal discharge, and visible blood in the urine. This is her second urinary tract infection; the first was about 2 years ago and cleared with antibiotics.

She has mild intermittent asthma and uses albuterol 2 puffs as needed, with no recent flares. She takes an oral contraceptive pill daily. She reports a sulfa allergy that causes a rash, so trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole will be avoided. She has had no new sexual partners.

She lives alone and has limited social support. Her family lives out of state and she has no one nearby to check on her if she gets worse. She works from home as a bookkeeper and has no car at the moment, so she relies on pharmacy delivery.

Vitals today: BP 112/70, HR 78, temperature 98.6 F. She appears comfortable. Mild suprapubic tenderness is present. There is no costovertebral angle tenderness and the rest of the abdomen is soft. Urine dipstick is positive for leukocyte esterase and nitrite with trace blood. Urine pregnancy test is negative. A urine culture was sent.

Impression: Uncomplicated urinary tract infection in a nonpregnant woman. Her asthma is well controlled.

Recommendations: Start nitrofurantoin 100 mg twice daily for 5 days, taken with food. Phenazopyridine 200 mg three times daily for 2 days for the burning, and I warned her that it turns the urine orange. Drink plenty of fluids. Continue albuterol as needed and her contraceptive pill. Because she lives alone, the pharmacy will deliver the antibiotic today, the clinic nurse will call her in 2 days to check her symptoms, and she gave me the number of a coworker she can text if she gets worse. She will call or message us sooner for fever, flank pain, vomiting, or symptoms that are not improving after 48 to 72 hours, and we will review the urine culture result with her.

She has mild intermittent asthma, a sulfa allergy, and lives alone with limited social support. Vitals were normal, she has mild suprapubic tenderness, and the urine dipstick was positive for leukocyte esterase and nitrite with a negative pregnancy test. The diagnosis is an uncomplicated urinary tract infection, treated with nitrofurantoin and phenazopyridine, with pharmacy delivery, a nurse call in 2 days, and return precautions arranged because she lives alone.

note:
Reason for consult: Positive interferon-gamma release assay found during pre-biologic screening. Requesting service: hospital medicine, at the request of rheumatology.

HPI: The patient is an 80-year-old female with rheumatoid arthritis who was admitted 4 days ago with cellulitis of the left lower leg, now improving on cefazolin 2 g IV every 8 hours. Rheumatology wants to start adalimumab after discharge, and screening showed a positive QuantiFERON. She returned 5 weeks ago from a 3-month stay with relatives in a country with a high burden of tuberculosis. She denies cough, hemoptysis, fever, night sweats, and weight loss, and she reports no known contact with anyone who has active tuberculosis. She has never been treated for tuberculosis and does not recall any earlier TB testing.

Other history: hypothyroidism. Medications: methotrexate 10 mg once weekly, folic acid 1 mg daily, and levothyroxine 88 mcg daily. No known drug allergies. She does not drink alcohol.

Exam: BP 134/72, HR 76, temperature 98.1 F, SpO2 97% on room air. She is comfortable and the left lower leg shows improving erythema. Her lungs are clear without crackles. No lymphadenopathy.

Data: QuantiFERON-TB Gold positive. Chest X-ray shows no infiltrate, cavity, or pleural effusion. AST 24 and ALT 19. Hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV screening results are pending.

Impression: Latent tuberculosis infection with no symptoms and no imaging findings of active disease.

Recommendations:
- No sputum testing or airborne isolation is needed given no symptoms and a normal chest X-ray.
- Treat with rifampin 600 mg daily for 4 months, starting at discharge. Check AST and ALT at baseline and monthly while she is also on methotrexate.
- Rifampin lowers levothyroxine levels, so check a TSH in 6 weeks and adjust the dose if needed.
- Hold methotrexate while she is on IV antibiotics for cellulitis; rheumatology to decide on restarting.
- Rheumatology can start adalimumab after at least 1 month of rifampin, once the hepatitis and HIV screens return.
- Infectious disease clinic follow-up in 4 weeks.
summary: An 80-year-old female with rheumatoid arthritis, hospitalized for left lower leg cellulitis, was seen in infectious disease consultation for a positive QuantiFERON found before planned adalimumab, after returning from a 3-month stay in a high tuberculosis burden country. She denies cough, hemoptysis, fever, night sweats, and weight loss, and her chest X-ray shows no infiltrate or cavity. The impression is latent tuberculosis infection with no sign of active disease. Rifampin 600 mg daily for 4 months is recommended starting at discharge with liver and TSH monitoring, methotrexate is held during IV antibiotics, and adalimumab can start after at least 1 month of rifampin.

note:
This is a hospitalist progress note dictated on hospital day 2 for a 56-year-old female admitted with an upper gastrointestinal bleed. She came in yesterday with 2 days of black tarry stools and one episode of coffee-ground emesis, felt lightheaded when she stood up, and arrived with a heart rate of 112 and a blood pressure of 98/58. Hemoglobin on arrival was 7.4, correction, 7.1, I misread the first printout, and she received 2 units of packed red blood cells with a post-transfusion hemoglobin of 8.9 this morning. Overnight she had no further black stools or vomiting, and she denies chest pain, shortness of breath, syncope, and abdominal pain at this time.

Social history is important here. She works night shifts as a certified nursing assistant on a rotating schedule, so she eats and sleeps at irregular times and often misses doses of her medicines. She told the team she stopped taking her omeprazole 20 mg about 3 months ago because she could not afford it, and she has been stretching out her metformin for the same reason. For back pain from work she has been taking over-the-counter naproxen, she first said 220 mg once in a while, correction, she takes two tablets, 440 mg, twice a day for the past 2 months. She does not drink alcohol, does not smoke, and takes no blood thinners, and she has no prior history of ulcers.

Past medical history includes type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and GERD. Home medications before admission were metformin 1000 mg twice daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, the omeprazole she was not taking, and the naproxen. No known drug allergies.

Current inpatient medications: pantoprazole, which was 40 mg IV once daily after the 80 mg bolus on admission and was increased this morning to 40 mg IV twice daily after the endoscopy findings, and sliding scale insulin. Lisinopril and metformin are being held and the naproxen has been stopped.

Vital signs this morning: temperature 98.4 F, heart rate 88, blood pressure 122/74, respiratory rate 16, oxygen saturation 97% on room air. On exam she is comfortable, the conjunctival pallor is improved, the abdomen is soft and non-tender with no guarding, and there is no hepatosplenomegaly. The rectal exam yesterday showed melena. Labs today: hemoglobin 8.9, platelets 312, INR 1.0, BUN 38 down from 52, creatinine 1.0, glucose 210, and A1c 8.4%.

Upper endoscopy this morning showed a 1.2 centimeter gastric ulcer in the antrum with a visible vessel, treated with epinephrine injection and two hemoclips with good hemostasis. Biopsies were taken for H pylori and the result is pending.

Assessment and plan by problem. Problem one, upper GI bleed from a gastric ulcer, most likely related to the naproxen. Continue pantoprazole 40 mg IV twice daily for 72 hours, then switch to 40 mg by mouth twice daily for 8 weeks. Permanently stop naproxen and avoid all NSAIDs. Keep her NPO today, then clear liquids this evening and advance the diet tomorrow. Check hemoglobin every 8 hours and transfuse for a hemoglobin under 7. Follow up the H pylori biopsy and treat if positive. Repeat endoscopy in 8 weeks to confirm healing. Problem two, acute blood loss anemia, as above. Problem three, type 2 diabetes with an A1c of 8.4%, continue to hold metformin while inpatient, continue sliding scale insulin, and resume metformin 1000 mg twice daily at discharge. Problem four, hypertension, blood pressure is now normal, continue to hold lisinopril today and restart it tomorrow if her systolic pressures stay above 130. Problem five, medication cost and adherence. Social work and pharmacy are consulted for low-cost generic options, 90-day supplies, and meds-to-beds delivery so that she leaves with her pantoprazole in hand, plus a pill organizer and dosing times lined up with her sleep schedule, taking the pantoprazole 30 minutes before the first meal after she wakes. Follow up with primary care in 1 week and the GI clinic in 8 weeks. Likely discharge tomorrow if the hemoglobin is stable.
summary: A 56-year-old female on hospital day 2 was admitted with an upper gastrointestinal bleed after 2 days of black tarry stools and coffee-ground emesis, with hemoglobin 7.1 on arrival and 8.9 after 2 units of red cells. She had been taking over-the-counter naproxen 440 mg twice a day and had stopped omeprazole because of cost, and she works rotating night shifts. Upper endoscopy showed a gastric ulcer with a visible vessel treated with epinephrine injection and hemoclips. Pantoprazole was increased to 40 mg IV twice daily, naproxen stopped permanently, lisinopril and metformin held, and social work and pharmacy involved for medication cost, with repeat endoscopy in 8 weeks.

note:
Visit modality: synchronous video visit, about 30 minutes. A professional Spanish medical interpreter joined by video for the entire visit, which the patient preferred over using a family member. The patient is a 65-year-old female with chronic kidney disease and type 2 diabetes who has hyperkalemia while taking lisinopril.

History: Her primary care physician found a potassium of 5.9 on routine labs 4 days ago and referred her urgently. Through the interpreter she reports no muscle weakness, palpitations, chest pain, nausea, or decreased urination. She says that over the past 3 months she began using a salt substitute on all her food to cut down on salt because of her blood pressure, and she eats bananas and oranges every day. She takes no NSAIDs or herbal products.

Medications, reviewed by holding the bottles up to the camera: lisinopril 40 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, metformin 500 mg twice daily, and atorvastatin 20 mg at bedtime. No known drug allergies.

Home data: BP 138/80 and pulse 72 this morning on her home cuff. Her last clinic labs showed creatinine 1.4, eGFR 44, and potassium 5.9, and a repeat potassium yesterday at an outpatient lab was 5.7. An ECG at her primary care office on the day of the first result showed no peaked T waves.

Limited video exam: She appears comfortable, speaks in full sentences, has no respiratory distress or facial swelling, and moves both arms normally.

Impression: Hyperkalemia, most likely from lisinopril combined with a potassium-containing salt substitute and a high-potassium diet, in the setting of chronic kidney disease stage 3b with an eGFR of 44. No symptoms or ECG changes of hyperkalemia.

Next steps, explained through the interpreter with teach-back:
- Stop the salt substitute completely, since it contains potassium chloride.
- Reduce lisinopril from 40 mg to 20 mg daily.
- Low-potassium diet handout in Spanish; limit bananas, oranges, potatoes, and tomatoes.
- Repeat basic metabolic panel in 3 days at the lab nearest her home, and again in 1 week.
- Continue amlodipine, metformin, and atorvastatin unchanged.
- Go to the emergency department right away for palpitations, muscle weakness, or fainting.
- Nephrology follow-up by video in 2 weeks with an interpreter booked.
summary: A 65-year-old female with chronic kidney disease and type 2 diabetes was seen by video with a professional Spanish interpreter for hyperkalemia while taking lisinopril, with potassium 5.9 and a repeat of 5.7. She denies muscle weakness, palpitations, chest pain, nausea, and decreased urination, and an ECG showed no peaked T waves. She uses a salt substitute and eats high-potassium foods, and her eGFR is 44. The impression is hyperkalemia from lisinopril, the salt substitute, and diet, so lisinopril was reduced from 40 mg to 20 mg daily, the salt substitute stopped, and repeat basic metabolic panels ordered in 3 days and 1 week.
